book_title: The Negative Working Capital Machine: How McKesson Turns Pennies Into Billions
question: How does a distributor earning a 1.54% GAAP operating margin generate $5.41 billion in annual Free Cash Flow and an extraordinary return on invested capital?

epigraph.quote: In high-velocity logistics, the balance sheet is the real income statement; negative working capital turns growth from a cash drain into a cash fountain.
epigraph.author: Working Capital Forensics Principle

web_blocks.html: McKesson runs a coast-to-coast network of automated distribution centers, ultra-cold specialty hubs, and forward depots. It delivers next-morning to tens of thousands of pharmacies, hospitals, and clinics [1, 18]. Under the federal Drug Supply Chain Security Act (DSCSA), every package needs unit-level electronic track-and-trace data from maker to dispenser [1]. Staying compliant takes ongoing spending on barcode robotics, warehouse software, and cold-chain gear. Total capex was $745 million in FY2026 ($436 million PP&E and $309 million software), or just 0.18% of sales [2]. Over 60% of that capex funds supply-chain upgrades, automated picking, and ultra-cold storage for cell therapies and GLP-1s [8, 19].

On procurement, McKesson pools generic buying power through ClarusONE, its joint venture with Walmart. That mirrors Cardinal Health's Red Oak Sourcing venture with CVS Health [22]. This scale wins deep generic discounts while passing through branded prices under fee-for-service deals [18, 22]. Independent and chain pharmacies rely on daily auto-replenishment to avoid tying up cash in slow stock. McKesson's hubs thus act as shared regional vaults for the U.S. pharmacy system [18].

web_blocks.title: Unit Economics: The FY2026 Per-$100 Revenue Waterfall

web_blocks.html: To see McKesson's unit economics clearly, trace every $100 of FY2026 revenue ($403,430 million) to Net Income ($5,099 million) and Free Cash Flow ($5,410 million) [2]. Cost of sales takes $96.39 per $100 ($388,880 million), leaving $3.61 in GAAP gross profit ($14,550 million) [2]. Operating expenses ($8,096 million), net restructuring ($245 million), and litigation credits (-$3 million) absorb $2.07 per $100. That yields $1.54 in GAAP operating income ($6,212 million) [2]. After $0.06 of interest ($247 million), $0.06 of other income ($236 million), and $0.27 of taxes ($1,102 million), McKesson keeps $1.26 in GAAP net income per $100 [2].

web_blocks.takeaway: Out of $403,430M in FY2026 revenue, McKesson converts $6,212M of GAAP operating income (1.54% margin) into $6,155M of operating cash flow and $5,410M of Free Cash Flow (106% conversion of GAAP net income) because capex is just 0.18% of sales.

web_blocks.title: The Negative Working Capital Flywheel & Credit Risk Management

web_blocks.html: The secret to McKesson's cash machine sits on its balance sheet. On March 31, 2026, McKesson held $27,985 million in net receivables (~25 days sales) and $24,207 million in inventories (~23 days on hand) [2]. Those $52,192 million in assets were funded by $59,973 million in drafts and accounts payable (~56 days payable) [2]. McKesson collects from pharmacies and hospitals faster than it pays drugmakers. Net trade working capital is therefore negative by $7,781 million [2]. As volume grows, payables rise faster than receivables and stock, turning growth into a cash source rather than a drain.

That working-capital engine carries credit risk when retail pharmacy chains stumble. During Rite Aid's bankruptcy, McKesson booked a $189 million pre-tax bad-debt charge in Q1 FY2026 before recognizing a $206 million pre-tax credit upon resolution [2, 9, 11]. Importantly, McKesson's negative working capital is genuine supplier float—not off-balance-sheet accounts-receivable factoring—with zero factoring facilities disclosed in its FY2026 Form 10-K or Q2 FY2027 Form 10-Q [1, 2]. On a 90-day year-end basis in the FY2026 10-K, customer receivables stood at 22 days, inventories at 24 days, and drafts and accounts payable at 59 days; by September 30, 2026, drafts and accounts payable reached $67,761 million against $30,806 million of receivables and $28,217 million of inventories [1, 15]. Meanwhile, Medical-Surgical Solutions (Wellverse) showed unit-economics friction in Q2 FY2027, with adjusted operating profit falling 10% YoY to $225 million on ambulatory product-mix headwinds, even as consolidated 6M FY2027 Free Cash Flow reached $2.6 billion ($2.9 billion in Q2 alone) [5, 8].

web_blocks.title: Why GLP-1s Dilute Percentage Margin Yet Grow Profit Dollars
paragraphs: In Q2 FY2027, GLP-1 revenue jumped 26% YoY to $16 billion in one quarter (~$64B annualized) [8]. Because GLP-1s have high prices, cold-chain needs, and capped fees, they lower McKesson's gross margin percentage [8, 19].

As CFO Kenny Cheung noted on the Q2 FY2027 call, gross profit dollars and operating leverage matter most. Consolidated operating expenses as a share of gross profit fell ~141 bps YoY in Q2 FY2027, proving scale absorbs GLP-1 volume profitably [8].

web_blocks.html: In sum, negative working capital and low capex turn a 1.54% GAAP operating margin into 106% free cash flow conversion [2]. Each new dollar of specialty or GLP-1 volume rides on existing automated rails, lifting cash generation without heavy new capital.

book_paragraphs: Here is one of the most surprising truths in finance: a business keeping only $1.54 in operating profit per $100 of sales can still be a top cash machine [2]. How is that possible? You have to look past the income statement and open the balance sheet. In high-speed distribution, cash timing matters more than headline margin.

Let's trace $100 flowing through McKesson in fiscal 2026 [2]. Out of that $100, $96.39 goes straight out to drugmakers like Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, and generic firms [2]. That leaves $3.61 of gross profit [2]. Next, McKesson pays its 43,000 staff, runs refrigerated trucks, maintains warehouses, and covers restructuring—another $2.07 [1, 2]. That leaves $1.54 in GAAP operating income [2]. After a small slice for interest and taxes, $1.26 drops to net income [2].

If you stopped there, McKesson might look thin and fragile. Now look at cash timing. When McKesson ships a pallet of drugs to a pharmacy or hospital, it collects cash in about 25 days [2]. Inventory sits in the warehouse for only 23 days, turning sixteen times a year [2]. Yet McKesson pays its drug-manufacturing suppliers in roughly 56 days [2]. That 8-day gap between collecting cash and paying suppliers powers the entire model.

Do the math with me. Receivables of $28.0 billion plus inventory of $24.2 billion equal $52.2 billion [2]. Against that, accounts payable sit at $60.0 billion [2]. That creates a negative $7.8 billion working capital gap [2]. Every time sales grow by $10 billion, suppliers effectively hand McKesson a few hundred million dollars in interest-free float. Meanwhile, total capex—for picking hubs, DSCSA scanners, cold vaults, and software—cost just $745 million in fiscal 2026, under 0.2% of sales [2]. The result? $6.16 billion in operating cash flow and $5.41 billion in Free Cash Flow—106% of GAAP net income, even after $684 million in opioid cash payouts [2].

Of course, extending 22 to 25 days of credit on $403 billion of sales means watching who owes you money. When Rite Aid filed for bankruptcy, McKesson took a $189 million bad-debt charge in Q1 fiscal 2026 before recovering most of it later [9, 11]. Just as important, forensic checks of the FY2026 10-K and Q2 FY2027 10-Q confirm McKesson uses zero off-balance-sheet receivables factoring—its $67.8 billion payable float as of September 30, 2026 is pure supplier credit [1, 15]. Generic sourcing also matters. Through ClarusONE, its venture with Walmart, McKesson pools generic buying power to earn wider spreads than on branded pills [22]. By contrast, Medical-Surgical's 10% Q2 FY2027 profit dip ($225 million) on ambulatory mix friction shows why separating Wellverse sharpens the core unit economics [5].

This also settles the Wall Street debate over GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. In Q2 fiscal 2027, McKesson moved $16 billion of GLP-1s in ninety days—up 26% YoY and 8% sequentially [8]. Critics worry that pricey, cold-chain GLP-1s with capped fees dilute gross margin percentage [19]. That is true, and misses the point. McKesson spends dollars, not percentages. As CFO Kenny Cheung noted in November 2026, operating expenses as a share of gross profit fell 141 bps YoY [8]. Extra GLP-1 volume rides on the same trucks and software, dropping cash straight to profit. That is why unit economics keep improving even as the revenue mix shifts.

Think about what DSCSA serialization also does for McKesson's moat. Federal law requires unit-level electronic tracking for every prescription bottle from factory to pharmacy [1]. Small regional wholesalers struggle to afford the scanners, cold vaults, and software needed for compliance. McKesson spent $745 million on capex in fiscal 2026, yet that was only 0.18% of sales [2]. Scale turns a heavy regulatory burden into a tiny cost per package.

Keep that number in mind: less than two-tenths of one percent of sales in capital spending [2]. Most industrial businesses spend 4% to 8% of revenue just to maintain their plants. Because McKesson runs on negative working capital and tiny capex, 106% of GAAP net income turned into free cash flow in fiscal 2026 [2]. That cash funds buybacks and specialty acquisitions without straining the balance sheet.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Never confuse a thin operating margin percentage with a weak business. When a distributor turns stock 16 times a year on negative $7.8 billion of working capital, a 1.5% margin yields huge returns on capital—and a moat no startup can undercut.
